title: Distant M5.5-5.9 earthquake counts fell in the first six hours after 125 M7.5+ events in ComCat, 2001-2024
abstract: We tested whether a distant earthquake count deficit was limited to early hours and smaller catalog events. We used a fixed ComCat snapshot with 12,848 M5.5+ earthquakes in 2000-2025. Centers were 125 M7.5+ events in 2001-2024. At distances above 1000 km, M5.5-5.9 counts were 22 in the first six hours after centers and 49 in the six hours before them. The after/before ratio was 0.449, with a conditional 95% year-bootstrap interval of 0.216-0.791. A shared within-year shift test gave a lower-tail p-value of 0.00195. Later windows gave ratios near one. However, M6+ counts also fell in the early window, and the magnitude-band contrast was unclear (p=0.643). The result supports an early catalog count deficit. It does not identify missed detections or physical suppression. This is a targeted follow-up that uses the same source as prior campaign work. Small counts, mixed magnitudes, event dependence, catalog changes and the shift assumption limit the result. Code, aggregate evidence, source hashes, a count audit and a chart are included. External source records stay outside the bundle.

display.caption: Distant count ratios in mirrored time windows and the primary shift test. Bars are conditional 95% year-bootstrap intervals. The magnitude contrast was unclear. Credit: USGS ComCat and contributing seismic networks.

citations.reason: Five-day paired low-count evidence motivates an early-hour and magnitude-band test. Same source and centers; not independent confirmation.
